kurals.tamil:
மறைப்பேன்மன் யானிஃதோ நோயை இறைப்பவர்க்கு
ஊற்றுநீர் போல மிகும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Maraippaenman yaaniqdhoa noayai iraippavarkku
ootruneer poala mikum.
kurals.meaning: I would hide this pain of love from others, but like the water of a spring that rises the more it is drawn, it only swells the more I try to hide it.
kurals.elementary: Think of a well in a garden: every bucket you pull out, the spring at the bottom fills it up again, even higher. The wife in this verse misses her husband, and she tries to keep her sadness a secret, but every time she pushes it down, it bubbles back up, bigger than before.
kurals.university: Chapter 117 belongs to the karpiyal (married love) and follows the husband’s departure in Chapter 116; its title joins padar (படர், the anguish of longing), melindhu (மெலிந்து, growing thin) and irangal (இரங்கல், lamenting), and commentators read most of its couplets as the heroine’s replies to her confidante (tōḻi), who urges her to bear the separation quietly. The image turns on iṟaippavarkku (இறைப்பவர்க்கு, ‘for those who bail or draw water’) and ūṟṟunīr (ஊற்றுநீர், spring water): concealment works like drawing from a spring, which only makes it flow faster. Man (மன்) is a particle of unrealised wish, ‘I would indeed hide it, but…’, and nōy (நோய், ‘sickness’) is the standard Kural word for love-pain. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah both gloss ‘the more I hide it, the more it grows’, and Pope renders: ‘I would my pain conceal, but see! it surging swells, / As streams to those that draw from ever-springing wells.’ The text is identical on ytamizh.com and thirukkural.net.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In one of her best-known songs Mirabai cries that she has gone mad with love and that no one knows her pain, which only the one who has suffered such a wound can understand.
hinduism.explanation: Mira’s longing for Krishna overflows every attempt to keep it private, and she lets it pour out in song.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Mira finds that love-pain cannot be kept hidden; it rises and spills into the open.
hinduism.source: Mirabai, pada ‘Hey ri main to prem diwani’ (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous bhakti song, not checked against a translation this session; it matches the overflowing, unhideable pain, though Mira chooses to proclaim it rather than trying to hide it.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name. But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.”
christianity.explanation: Jeremiah resolves to keep silent, but what he holds inside burns until he can no longer contain it.
christianity.tie_back: The same failure of concealment as the Kural: the harder the speaker holds it in, the more it presses to come out.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close match in the dynamics of failed suppression, though the burden is a prophetic word, not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And he turned away from them and said, ‘Oh, my sorrow over Joseph,’ and his eyes became white from grief, for he was [of that] a suppressor.”
islam.explanation: Jacob holds in his grief for his lost son, yet it breaks out in his words and even whitens his eyes.
islam.tie_back: Jacob is a ‘suppressor’ of sorrow whose sorrow still shows, just as the Kural’s heroine hides a pain that keeps welling up.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International); a strong match for suppressed grief that cannot stay hidden, though the grief is a father’s, not a lover’s.

judaism.quote_or_event: “I was dumb with silence; I held my peace, had no comfort; and my pain was held in check. My heart waxed hot within me; while I was musing, the fire kindled; Then spoke I with my tongue.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist tries to keep silent about his pain, but the restraint only makes it burn hotter until he must speak.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s spring in another image: pain that is held in check grows until it breaks out.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close structural parallel of suppression intensifying pain, though the psalm’s pain is not romantic.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Whoever is overcome by this wretched and sticky craving, his sorrows grow like grass after the rains.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha teaches that sorrow fed by craving does not shrink on its own but keeps sprouting and spreading.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds her love-pain multiplying like spring water; the Dhammapada traces the same growth of sorrow to attachment itself.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; matches the image of sorrow that keeps growing, though the Buddhist answer is to uproot craving rather than to hide it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “O Gautama, in the innermost heart there grows a plant which brings forth poisonous fruit; how have you torn it out?”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, the plant growing in the heart is ‘love of existence’, which Gautama has torn out by the roots.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has a love growing in her heart that only spreads when hidden; the Jain image is the same hidden growth, though its cure is uprooting.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; a real image of an inward attachment that grows unseen, but the Jain text treats it as something to destroy, not to conceal.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Euripides’ Hippolytus, Phaedra hides her love for her stepson until she is wasting away and refusing food, and her nurse finally draws the secret from her.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra’s concealment does not quiet her passion; it consumes her body until it can no longer be kept in.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Phaedra lives out the Kural’s complaint: the love she hides grows stronger and shows itself despite her.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the play’s well-known situation, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel for hidden love that will not stay hidden, though Phaedra’s love is illicit, unlike the Kural’s wife’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: La Rochefoucauld observes that there is no disguise that can long hide love where it exists, nor feign it where it does not.
philosophy.explanation: For the moralist, love is one passion that resists every effort at concealment.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine discovers exactly this: her attempt to hide love only reveals it.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known maxim, not checked word for word this session; a near match in claim, though without the Kural’s image of concealment making it grow.

kurals.tamil:
கரத்தலும் ஆற்றேன்இந் நோயைநோய் செய்தார்க்கு
உரைத்தலும் நாணுத் தரும்.
kurals.transliteration:
Karaththalum aatraeninh noayainoai seydhaarkku
uraiththalum naanuth tharum.
kurals.meaning: I cannot keep this love-pain hidden, and yet to tell it to the one who caused it fills me with shame.
kurals.elementary: Imagine you miss someone so much that everyone can see it on your face, but when you think of phoning them to say ‘I miss you’, you feel too shy. You are stuck in the middle: you cannot hide it and you cannot say it. That is exactly how the wife in this verse feels.
kurals.university: The couplet sets two failures side by side with the double -um (‘both… and’): karattal (கரத்தல், concealing) is beyond her strength (āṟṟēṉ, ஆற்றேன், ‘I am unable’), and uraittal (உரைத்தல், telling) brings nāṇ (நாண், modesty, shame). The phrase nōy ceytārkku (நோய் செய்தார்க்கு, ‘to the one who caused the sickness’) is pointed: the cure and the cause are the same person. Puliyur Kesikan reads the telling as sending a message (tūtu) to the absent husband, which modesty forbids, while Solomon Pappaiah modernises it to writing or telephoning. Nāṇ is one of the defining virtues of the Tamil heroine, and the Kamattuppal repeatedly stages its struggle with kāmam (desire), most fully in Chapter 114 and in the next couplet. Pope: ‘I cannot hide this pain of mine, yet shame restrains / When I would tell it out to him who caused my pains.’ The words are identical on both base sources, with only a spacing difference at ஆற்றேன்இந்.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Wasting with love for King Dushyanta, Shakuntala is too shy to declare herself, until her friends persuade her to write him a love-letter, which she composes in deep embarrassment.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s heroine is caught between a longing everyone can see and the modesty that keeps her from speaking.
hinduism.tie_back: Shakuntala stands exactly where the Kural’s heroine stands: unable to hide her love and ashamed to tell it to its cause.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; a strong situational match, though Shakuntala is not yet married and her beloved is present, not absent.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I charge you, O daughters of Jerusalem, if ye find my beloved, that ye tell him, that I am sick of love.”
christianity.explanation: The bride cannot keep her love-sickness to herself, yet she sends others to tell her beloved rather than telling him herself.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she cannot hide the sickness and can only send word of it through others.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close match in love-sickness reported through messengers, though the verse does not name shame as the reason.

islam.quote_or_event: “He said, ‘I only complain of my suffering and my grief to Allāh, and I know from Allāh that which you do not know.’”
islam.explanation: Jacob will not lay out his grief before those around him; he brings his complaint only to God.
islam.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Jacob carries a pain he cannot hide but will not voice to people; unlike her, he has a listener to whom it is no shame to speak.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International); it matches a grief that cannot be hidden yet is not spoken to others, but the restraint is devotion, not modesty.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Oh that thou wert as my brother, That sucked the breasts of my mother! When I should find thee without, I would kiss thee; Yea, and none would despise me.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song wishes she could show her love openly without incurring the scorn that convention would bring.
judaism.tie_back: She shares the Kural’s bind: love she cannot hide, but cannot express openly without shame.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a genuine conflict between love and public shame, though the shame is social rather than modesty before the beloved himself.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Ummadanti Jataka, King Sivi falls in love with the beautiful Ummadanti and, too ashamed to speak of it, keeps it to himself until he grows sick with longing and his minister guesses the cause.
buddhism.explanation: The king’s concealed passion shows itself in his wasting body, while shame keeps him from naming it.
buddhism.tie_back: As in the Kural, the love-sickness cannot be hidden, yet shame forbids saying it aloud.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the story’s outline, not checked against Cowell’s translation this session; the hidden, shameful love-sickness matches, though the king’s love is for another man’s wife and he ends by mastering it.

jainism.quote_or_event: “A stupid, ignorant sinner who never fixes his thoughts on the soul’s benefit and eternal welfare, but sinks down through hatred and the temptation of lust, will be ensnared as a fly is caught on glue.”
jainism.explanation: Kapila’s verses compare the person gripped by passion to a fly stuck fast in glue, unable to move either way.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is stuck just so: she can neither hide her love nor speak it; the Jain verse names that stuckness as the bondage of passion.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; only the image of being trapped connects to the Kural, and the Jain verse condemns the passion the Kural treats sympathetically.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Phaedra writes to Hippolytus that what modesty forbade her to say aloud, Love has commanded her to write, and that three times her tongue failed her when she tried to speak.
greek_mythology.explanation: Phaedra can neither keep silent nor speak face to face, so shame drives her to a letter.
greek_mythology.tie_back: This is the Kural’s double bind almost exactly: the love will not stay hidden, and shame stops the telling.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the opening of the letter, not checked against a translation this session; a close match in psychology, though Phaedra’s love is illicit, unlike the Kural’s wife’s.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Stendhal devotes a chapter of On Love to modesty (pudeur), arguing that it makes a woman suffer in silence rather than reveal her feelings, even to the man she loves.
philosophy.explanation: For Stendhal, modesty is a powerful inner restraint that holds back the expression of love.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural names the same force: nāṇ, which makes telling her beloved a source of shame.
philosophy.source: Stendhal, On Love, chapter on modesty (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Stendhal’s general argument, not checked against a translation this session; it addresses modesty restraining love but not the specific double bind of the couplet.

kurals.tamil:
காமமும் நாணும் உயிர்காவாத் தூங்கும்என்
நோனா உடம்பின் அகத்து.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamamum naanum uyirkaavaath thoongumen
noanaa udampin akaththu.
kurals.meaning: Within my body, which can no longer bear it, love and shame hang from either end of a carrying pole, and my very life is that pole.
kurals.elementary: Have you seen someone carry two heavy buckets on a stick across their shoulders? The wife says her heart is like that stick: on one side hangs her love for her husband, on the other her shyness, and both are so heavy she feels she might break.
kurals.university: The central image is the kāvu (காவு) or kāvaḍi, a shoulder pole with loads at each end: uyir (உயிர், life) is the pole, and kāmam (காமம், desire) and nāṇ (நாண், modesty) hang (tūṅgum, தூங்கும்) in balance from it. Nōṉā uṭampu (நோனா உடம்பு) is ‘the body that cannot endure’, already worn thin by separation, which carries the whole apparatus. Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah spell out the two loads exactly as love-pain and the shame of not being able to tell it, linking this couplet to 1162; Kalaignar describes the suffering body itself as a kāvaḍi. The image is admired in the commentary tradition because the balance is the torment: neither load can be dropped without the other swinging. Pope: ‘My soul, like porter’s pole, within my wearied frame, / Sustains a two-fold burthen poised, of love and shame.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta, the exiled yaksha imagines his wife grown thin with separation, lying on one side of her bed like the last thin sliver of the waning moon.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa pictures the body of a separated wife worn down until it can barely hold her grief.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine speaks of the same body that can no longer bear its load of love.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known image, not checked against a translation this session; it matches the wasting body but not the twin burden of love and shame.

christianity.quote_or_event: “For my life is spent with grief, and my years with sighing: my strength faileth because of mine iniquity, and my bones are consumed.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist describes grief that has worn down his strength and consumed his very frame.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the speaker feels sorrow as a weight his body can no longer carry.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the body failing under grief matches, but the psalm ties it to iniquity rather than to love and shame.

islam.quote_or_event: “Our Lord, and burden us not with that which we have no ability to bear.”
islam.explanation: The closing prayer of Surat al-Baqarah asks God not to lay on believers a load beyond their capacity.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine describes just such a load: a body that cannot bear the double weight of love and shame.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International); it shares only the idea of an unbearable burden, and its context is religious obligation, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Stay ye me with dainties, refresh me with apples; For I am love-sick.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song asks to be held up and revived because love has made her faint.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she feels love as a physical weight her body can scarcely sustain.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); it captures love-sickness weakening the body, though there is no counterweight of shame and the lovers are not separated.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “From endearment springs grief, from endearment springs fear. For one who is wholly free from endearment there is no grief, whence then fear?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha traces both grief and fear to the root of affection for what is dear.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine carries two loads, desire and shame; the Dhammapada sees such twin burdens growing from a single root of attachment.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it pairs two afflictions arising from love, but grief and fear are not the Kural’s love and shame, and the verse counsels detachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Love, hatred, &c., are heavy fetters, attachment is a dangerous one; having regularly destroyed them, I live up to the rules of conduct.”
jainism.explanation: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, Gautama names love and its opposite as the heavy fetters that bind beings.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine feels love as a heavy load hung on her life; Jain teaching calls such love a heavy fetter to be cut.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; the shared idea is love as a heavy burden, but the Jain answer is renunciation, opposite to the Kural’s sympathy.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In her most famous poem Sappho describes love overwhelming her body: her tongue breaks, a thin fire runs under her skin, her eyes see nothing, she trembles and turns paler than grass, and seems to herself little short of dying.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho makes love a bodily crisis that the frame can scarcely survive.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also speaks of a body that cannot endure what love lays on it.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a very well-known poem, not checked against a translation this session; a strong parallel for love’s physical toll, though it lacks the counterweight of shame.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Plato’s Phaedrus the lover’s soul is a charioteer with two horses, one restrained by modesty and shame, the other driven wildly by desire, so that the soul is pulled painfully in two directions.
philosophy.explanation: Plato pictures the lover’s inner life as a strained balance between desire and shame.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s carrying pole is a Tamil version of the same picture: love on one side, shame on the other, and the self stretched between them.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous passage, not checked word for word this session; the opposition of desire and shame within the lover is a close match, though Plato wants shame to win.

kurals.tamil:
காமக் கடல்மன்னும் உண்டே அதுநீந்தும்
ஏமப் புணைமன்னும் இல்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamak kadalmannum undae adhuneendhum
aemap punaimannum il.
kurals.meaning: There is indeed a sea of love before me, but there is no safe raft on which to cross it.
kurals.elementary: Picture standing on a beach looking at a huge ocean you need to cross, but there is no boat, not even a little raft. That is how the wife feels about her love while her husband is away: it is as big as the sea, and the one who could carry her across is not here.
kurals.university: The couplet balances two clauses with the emphatic particle maṉṉum (மன்னும், ‘indeed’): there is (uṇṭē) a sea of kāmam, and there is no (il) ēmap puṇai (ஏமப் புணை), a ‘raft of safety’. Puṇai (புணை) is a float or raft, and ēmam (ஏமம்) means protection or security. Puliyur Kesikan identifies the missing raft as the husband himself, who alone could carry her across and is now absent, while Solomon Pappaiah reads the sea as love-pain that has outgrown the shame of the previous couplet. The sea image recurs at 1166 and 1167, and readers have long noted its echo of the Kural’s opening chapter (Kural 10), where the ‘great sea of births’ is crossed only by those who cling to the feet of God: here the ocean is love and no such crossing is available. Pope: ‘A sea of love, ’tis true, I see stretched out before, / But not the trusty bark that wafts to yonder shore.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Krishna tells Arjuna that even the worst of sinners, once in the boat of knowledge, will cross over the whole ocean of wrongdoing and misery.
hinduism.explanation: The Gita offers knowledge as the boat that carries a person across an otherwise impassable sea.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine faces a sea of love and finds no such boat; the Gita supplies the boat she lacks, but for a different ocean.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known verse, not checked against the As It Is wording this session; the sea-and-boat image matches closely, but the ocean is sin, not love.

christianity.quote_or_event: “But when he saw the wind boisterous, he was afraid; and beginning to sink, he cried, saying, Lord, save me.”
christianity.explanation: Peter, trying to cross the water to Jesus, begins to sink and cries out for rescue.
christianity.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Peter is in water too great for him and without anything to hold him up but the one he is trying to reach.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the image of sinking without support matches, though Peter is rescued and the sea is literal.

islam.quote_or_event: “[But] he said, ‘I will take refuge on a mountain to protect me from the water.’ [Noah] said, ‘There is no protector today from the decree of Allāh, except for whom He gives mercy.’ And the waves came between them, and he was among the drowned.”
islam.explanation: Noah’s son refuses the ark and looks for his own refuge, but there is none, and the waves separate him from his father.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also faces a flood with no means of safety, and waves of distance lie between her and the one she loves.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International); the absence of any safe refuge from a flood matches, but the story is one of judgment, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “Save me, O God; For the waters are come in even unto the soul. I am sunk in deep mire, where there is no standing; I am come into deep waters, and the flood overwhelmeth me.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist describes distress as deep water with no footing and no escape.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s sea of love is just such water: deep, overwhelming, and with nothing to keep her afloat.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close image of drowning without support, though the psalm’s distress is persecution, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: In the Simile of the Raft, the Buddha describes a man facing a great expanse of water with no ferry or bridge, who gathers grass and branches, binds them into a raft, and crosses safely to the far shore.
buddhism.explanation: The Dhamma is compared to a raft built for crossing a flood and then set down once the crossing is made.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine sees the same flood but has no raft; the Buddha’s simile supplies exactly the vessel she says is missing.
buddhism.source: Majjhima Nikaya 22, Alagaddupama Sutta (Simile of the Raft) (paraphrase)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous simile, not quoted from a translation this session; the image of crossing a flood by raft matches closely, but the flood is samsara, not love.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The body is the boat, life is the sailor, and the Circle of Births is the ocean which is crossed by the great sages.”
jainism.explanation: Gautama explains to Kesi that only a boat that does not leak reaches the far shore, and names the boat, the sailor and the ocean.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine has a sea before her and no boat; the Jain answer is that the disciplined body itself must become the vessel, though for the ocean of births, not of love.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; the ocean-and-boat image matches strongly, but the ocean in the Jain text is samsara and the crossing is liberation.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Poseidon wrecks the raft Odysseus built to leave Calypso, and he is left swimming for days in the open sea until the sea-goddess Ino gives him her veil to keep him afloat.
greek_mythology.explanation: Odysseus, trying to get home to his wife, loses his only means of crossing and is left at the mercy of the sea.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine is in the same plight from the other side: a sea separates the couple and the raft is gone.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode, not checked against a translation this session; the lost raft and the sea between spouses match, though the sea is literal.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Spinoza calls the human lack of power to govern the emotions ‘bondage’, explaining that a person under their sway is not his own master but lies at the mercy of fortune.
philosophy.explanation: For Spinoza, someone swept by passion has no secure footing of his own.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s sea without a raft is a picture of exactly this helplessness before a passion.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known passage, not checked word for word this session; it states the helplessness under passion but not the sea image or the absent beloved.

kurals.tamil:
துப்பின் எவனாவர் மன்கொல் துயர்வரவு
நட்பினுள் ஆற்று பவர்.
kurals.transliteration:
Thuppin evanaavar mankol thuyarvaravu
natpinul aatru pavar.
kurals.meaning: If he can bring me such sorrow while we are lovers, what would he do to me if he were my enemy?
kurals.elementary: Imagine your best friend forgets your birthday and it really hurts. You might say, ‘If this is how much my friend can hurt me, I would hate to see what an enemy could do!’ The wife is half-joking, half-hurt in the same way about her husband who has gone away.
kurals.university: The couplet is ironic reproach: the husband ‘accomplishes the coming of sorrow’ (tuyar varavu āṟṟupavar, துயர்வரவு ஆற்றுபவர்) even within naṭpu (நட்பு, friendship, intimacy), so what (evaṉ, எவன்) would he become in tuppu (துப்பு)? The commentators divide over tuppu: Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take it as ‘strength’, the power needed against a foe, while Solomon Pappaiah and Kalaignar take it directly as ‘enmity’ (pakai), and the sense is the same either way. Maṉ kol (மன்கொல்) adds wondering doubt. The reproach is affectionate rather than bitter, in keeping with the karpu ideal in which the wife complains of, but does not renounce, the absent husband. Pope: ‘Who work us woe in friendship’s trustful hour, / What will they prove when angry tempests lower?’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Shakuntala comes to Dushyanta’s court, the king, his memory clouded by a curse, denies he ever married her, and she reproaches him for treating with such cruelty the woman he had won with tender words.
hinduism.explanation: The very man who loved her becomes the source of her deepest wound.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Shakuntala finds that the one bound to her by love can hurt her more than any enemy.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known scene, not checked against a translation this session; the beloved as wounder matches, but Dushyanta’s rejection is far harsher than an absence.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Yea, mine own familiar friend, in whom I trusted, which did eat of my bread, hath lifted up his heel against me.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist laments that the wound came not from a stranger but from his trusted companion.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same complaint: the hurt comes from the one bound to her in love.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the wound from a friend matches, but the psalm describes betrayal, which is more than the husband’s absence.

islam.quote_or_event: “Oh, woe to me! I wish I had not taken that one as a friend.”
islam.explanation: On the Day of Judgment the wrongdoer laments the friendship that led him to ruin.
islam.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, more gently, also counts the sorrow that comes through a bond of friendship.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International); only the idea of harm through friendship connects, and the Qur’anic regret is far graver than the Kural’s loving reproach.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For it was not an enemy that taunted me, Then I could have borne it; Neither was it mine adversary that did magnify himself against me, Then I would have hid myself from him. But it was thou, a man mine equal, My companion, and my familiar friend.”
judaism.explanation: The psalmist says he could have endured an enemy’s hostility; it is the hurt from a close companion that is unbearable.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s comparison of friend and foe turned the same way: the wound from one who loves is the hardest to bear.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match in comparing the friend’s wound with an enemy’s, though the psalm describes betrayal rather than a lover’s absence.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Seek no intimacy with the beloved and also not with the unloved, for not to see the beloved and to see the unloved, both are painful.”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha observes that the beloved can cause pain just as surely as the disliked, simply by being absent.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine finds the same thing: the beloved, by being away, causes as much pain as an enemy could.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; it pairs pain from the beloved’s absence with pain from the unloved, close to the Kural’s friend-and-foe comparison, though the Buddhist conclusion is to avoid attachment.

jainism.quote_or_event: In Kapila’s verses a monk is told to quit his former connections and set his affection on nothing, for one who loves not even those who love him will be free from sin and hatred.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching sees affection itself as the channel through which suffering enters, and so advises withdrawing it.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine discovers that the bond of love is what lets her husband hurt her; the Jain text draws the renunciant’s conclusion from that same fact.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a verse read on sacred-texts.com this session; the link is only that love exposes one to pain, and the Jain counsel of detachment is the opposite of the Kural’s loyal complaint.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In Ovid’s Heroides, Ariadne, abandoned on the island of Naxos by Theseus, writes that she saved his life and was repaid with desertion, so that the man she helped has wounded her worse than any foe.
greek_mythology.explanation: Ariadne’s complaint is that her pain comes from the very person she loved and served.
greek_mythology.tie_back: She voices the Kural’s question: if love does this, what could enmity do?
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s situation, not checked against a translation this session; the wound from the beloved matches, though Theseus’s desertion is final and the Kural’s husband will return.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In Cicero’s On Friendship, Laelius reflects that friendships which break down often turn into bitter enmities, and that the hurt is the sharper because of the intimacy that preceded it.
philosophy.explanation: Cicero notes that closeness gives a friend unusual power to wound.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s rueful question rests on the same insight: love gives the beloved the power to cause the deepest pain.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a general theme of the dialogue, not checked against a translation this session and without a precise section number; only a partial fit, since the Kural describes no breach of friendship.

kurals.tamil:
இன்பம் கடல்மற்றுக் காமம் அஃதடுங்கால்
துன்பம் அதனிற் பெரிது.
kurals.transliteration:
Inpam kadalmatruk kaamam aqdhadungaal
thunpam adhanir peridhu.
kurals.meaning: The joy of love is as vast as the sea, but when love turns to torment, its sorrow is even greater than the sea.
kurals.elementary: When your best friend is with you, the fun feels as big as the ocean. But when they move far away, the missing-them feeling can seem even bigger than that ocean. The wife says love works like that: the happy part is huge, and the sad part is huger still.
kurals.university: The couplet sets inpam (இன்பம், joy) against tunpam (துன்பம், sorrow) with kaṭal (கடல், sea) as the unit of measure: love’s joy is a sea, and its pain, when it aṭuṅkāl (அடுங்கால், ‘when it torments’), is periṭu (பெரிது), greater than that. Maṟṟu (மற்று) marks the turn, ‘but then’. Mu. Varadarasanar and Puliyur Kesikan take the contrast as union versus separation, which fits the chapter’s setting. The sea of 1164 thus grows: there it was a sea without a raft, here the sorrow exceeds the sea. Pope: ‘A happy love’s sea of joy; but mightier sorrows roll / From unpropitious love athwart the troubled soul.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Gita Govinda, Radha, separated from Krishna after their joy together, is described as wasting with longing, feeling even moonlight and cool breezes as burning, while her friend pleads with Krishna to return.
hinduism.explanation: Jayadeva’s poem moves from the bliss of union to an anguish of separation that seems to fill the whole world.
hinduism.tie_back: Radha experiences the Kural’s arithmetic: love’s joy is great, but the pain of its loss feels greater still.
hinduism.source: Jayadeva, Gita Govinda, songs of Radha’s separation (paraphrase)
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the poem’s viraha sections, not checked against a translation this session; the swing from joy to greater sorrow matches, though the poem never states the comparison explicitly.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Even in laughter the heart is sorrowful; and the end of that mirth is heaviness.”
christianity.explanation: The proverb warns that joy can end in a sorrow that outweighs it.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine has lived this: love’s mirth has ended in a heaviness greater than the joy.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; joy ending in heaviness matches, but the proverb is general wisdom, not about love.

islam.quote_or_event: In Nizami’s Layla and Majnun, the brief joy of the young lovers’ first meeting gives way, after they are separated, to Majnun’s lifelong grief, which drives him to wander the desert.
islam.explanation: Nizami’s romance, read in Sufi tradition as an allegory of longing for the divine, makes the sorrow of separation far exceed the joy of union.
islam.tie_back: Majnun’s story is the Kural’s claim told as a life: love’s sorrow outgrows love’s joy.
islam._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the romance’s overall arc, not checked against a translation this session; a strong thematic match, though the work is Persian literature in an Islamic culture rather than scripture.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For love is strong as death, Jealousy is cruel as the grave; The flashes thereof are flashes of fire, A very flame of the LORD. Many waters cannot quench love, Neither can the floods drown it.”
judaism.explanation: The Song measures love against death, the grave and the floods, and finds love the stronger.
judaism.tie_back: Like the Kural, the Song uses the largest measures it knows, death and the floods, to show how vast love’s power is, including its power to hurt.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); it matches love measured against waters and floods, but celebrates love’s strength rather than weighing its sorrow against its joy.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “If one, longing for sensual pleasure, achieves it, yes, he’s enraptured at heart. The mortal gets what he wants. But if for that person, longing, desiring, the pleasures diminish, he’s shattered, as if shot with an arrow.”
buddhism.explanation: The Kama Sutta sets the rapture of getting what one desires against the shattering pain of losing it.
buddhism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s two-part comparison: love’s joy is great, but its loss strikes harder still.
buddhism.source: Sutta Nipata 4.1, Kama Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; a close structural match of rapture against shattering loss, though the sutta’s point is to avoid sensual desire altogether.

jainism.quote_or_event: “Pleasures bring only a moment’s happiness, but suffering for a very long time, intense suffering, but slight happiness; they are an obstacle to the liberation from existence, and are a very mine of evils.”
jainism.explanation: The two sons of the priest Bhrigu tell their father that the pain pleasures bring far outweighs the pleasure itself.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine makes the same reckoning from inside love: its sorrow is greater than its joy.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com; a near match in weighing pleasure’s joy against its greater suffering, though the Jain verse draws a renunciant conclusion the Kural does not.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Sappho calls Eros the ‘limb-loosener’ and names him ‘bittersweet’, a creature against whom there is no defence.
greek_mythology.explanation: Sappho’s coined word holds love’s sweetness and its bitterness in a single breath.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural measures the same two sides of love and finds the bitter part the larger.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous fragment, not checked against a translation this session; it pairs love’s sweetness and bitterness but does not say which is greater.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Schopenhauer argues that pain is positive and felt directly, while pleasure is merely the absence of pain, so that in any honest reckoning the suffering in life outweighs its enjoyment.
philosophy.explanation: For Schopenhauer, sorrow is always the heavier side of the scale.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine reaches the same verdict about love: its joy is a sea, but its sorrow is greater.
philosophy.source: Schopenhauer, ‘On the Sufferings of the World’ (Studies in Pessimism) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known essay, not checked against a translation this session; the claim that pain outweighs pleasure matches, though Schopenhauer generalises to all life, not love.

kurals.tamil:
காமக் கடும்புனல் நீந்திக் கரைகாணேன்
யாமத்தும் யானே உளேன்.
kurals.transliteration:
Kaamak kadumpunal neendhik karaikaanaen
yaamaththum yaanae ulaen.
kurals.meaning: I swim the fierce flood of love but see no shore; even in the middle of the night, I alone am awake.
kurals.elementary: Imagine swimming and swimming in a huge lake at night, looking for the edge, and never finding it, while everyone else is fast asleep in bed. That is how the wife feels: her missing-him feeling seems to have no end, and at midnight she is the only one still awake.
kurals.university: Kaṭum puṉal (கடும்புனல்) is a ‘fierce flood’ or torrent, extending the sea of 1164 and 1166 into a current she must swim; karai kāṇēṉ (கரைகாணேன்) is ‘I see no shore’. Yāmam (யாமம்) is the midnight watch, and yāṉē uḷēṉ (யானே உளேன்), ‘I alone am’, is read by all four modern glossators as ‘I alone remain awake’, while Pope’s commentary-based prose adds ‘still I live’, catching the other shade of uḷēṉ (‘I exist, I survive’). The couplet introduces the night theme that the next two couplets develop. Pope’s verse: ‘I swim the cruel tide of love, and can no shore descry, / In watches of the night, too, ’mid the waters, only I!’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Nala abandons Damayanti while she sleeps in the forest, she wakes alone in the night, searches for him in vain, and wanders through the wilderness crying out his name.
hinduism.explanation: Damayanti’s night of waking to find herself alone is one of the great scenes of separation in the Mahabharata.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Damayanti is the one left awake and alone in the night, with no end to her searching in sight.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous episode, not checked against a translation this session; the lonely night and endless search match, though Damayanti has been deliberately abandoned.

christianity.quote_or_event: “Deep calleth unto deep at the noise of thy waterspouts: all thy waves and thy billows are gone over me.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist, longing for God, feels himself overwhelmed by wave after wave.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also feels herself under a flood of longing that has no end.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the endless waves of longing match, but the longing is for God and there is no image of night or of searching for a shore.

islam.quote_or_event: “Or [they are] like darknesses within an unfathomable sea which is covered by waves, upon which are waves, over which are clouds - darknesses, some of them upon others. When one puts out his hand [therein], he can hardly see it.”
islam.explanation: The Qur’an describes a person without light as lost in a deep, dark sea, wave on wave, with nothing visible.
islam.tie_back: The heroine’s midnight flood with no shore in sight is the same picture of being lost in dark waters.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International); the image of a dark, shoreless sea matches strongly, but the verse describes unbelief, not love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “By night on my bed I sought him whom my soul loveth; I sought him, but I found him not.”
judaism.explanation: The beloved in the Song lies awake at night searching for her absent lover without finding him.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s heroine at midnight: awake, searching, and unable to reach the end of her longing.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close match in a woman’s sleepless night of longing for her absent beloved, though without the flood image.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “The misguided man in whom the thirty-six currents of craving strongly rush toward pleasurable objects, is swept away by the flood of his passionate thoughts.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada pictures craving as a set of currents that carry the mind away like a flood.
buddhism.tie_back: The heroine’s ‘fierce flood of love’ is this same current, and she, too, finds no shore.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the flood of passion matches the Kural’s image closely, though the verse is a warning against craving rather than a lover’s lament.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The flood is old age and death, which carry away living beings; Law is the island, the firm ground, the refuge, the most excellent shelter.”
jainism.explanation: Asked whether there is any firm ground for beings swept off by the great flood, Gautama names the Law as the island.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine swims a flood and sees no shore; the Jain text names a shore, but for the flood of birth and death rather than love.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com; the flood without firm ground matches, but the flood here is mortality and the island is the Jain Law.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Leander swims the Hellespont each night to reach Hero, guided by her lamp, until one stormy night the lamp is blown out and he drowns before reaching the shore.
greek_mythology.explanation: The story of Hero and Leander makes love literally a night swim through a dangerous sea.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine swims love’s flood at midnight and sees no shore, just as Leander fails to reach his.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous story, which Ovid’s letters anticipate and later poets (e.g. Musaeus) complete; the night swim matches strikingly, though the Kural’s flood is a metaphor.

philosophy.quote_or_event: In The Anatomy of Melancholy, Robert Burton lists among the symptoms of love-melancholy that lovers cannot sleep, but lie awake through the night sighing and thinking of the absent beloved.
philosophy.explanation: Burton’s encyclopaedic study treats sleeplessness as a classic sign of love-sickness.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine, alone and awake at midnight, shows exactly this symptom.
philosophy.source: Robert Burton, The Anatomy of Melancholy, Part 3, Section 2 (Love-Melancholy) (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the section’s general content, not checked word for word this session; it matches the sleepless night, but is a clinical catalogue rather than a lover’s voice.

kurals.tamil:
மன்னுயிர் எல்லாம் துயிற்றி அளித்திரா
என்னல்லது இல்லை துணை.
kurals.transliteration:
Mannuyir ellaam thuyitri aliththiraa
ennalladhu illai thunai.
kurals.meaning: Poor night! It has lulled every living thing to sleep, and now it has no companion but me.
kurals.elementary: Have you ever been the only one awake in the house at night? Everyone is asleep, it is very quiet, and you feel like it is just you and the dark. The wife feels so lonely that she starts feeling sorry for the night itself, because the only friend the night has left is her.
kurals.university: The couplet personifies irā (இரா, night): it has put to sleep (tuyiṟṟi, துயிற்றி) all ‘abiding lives’ (maṉṉuyir, மன்னுயிர்), and now has no tuṇai (துணை, companion) except (allatu) me. Aḷittu (அளித்து) is read in two ways: Mu. Varadarasanar and Solomon Pappaiah take it as ‘pitiable’ (‘this night is to be pitied’), while Pope’s commentary-based prose takes it as ‘graciously’ (‘the night which graciously lulls to sleep all living creatures’). The irony is turned inward: by pitying the night’s solitude the heroine reveals her own. Kalaignar makes it an address, ‘O Night!’. Pope’s verse: ‘All living souls in slumber soft she steeps; / But me alone kind night for her companing keeps!’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: Searching Lanka by night while the city sleeps, Hanuman at last finds Sita in the Ashoka grove, worn with grief, keeping a lonely watch among sleeping guards.
hinduism.explanation: Sita, separated from Rama, is the one wakeful figure in a slumbering city.
hinduism.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, she keeps company with the night while all others sleep.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the Sundara Kanda search, not checked against a translation this session; details of timing are simplified, and only the situation of a lone wakeful grieving wife matches.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I watch, and am as a sparrow alone upon the house top.”
christianity.explanation: The afflicted psalmist lies awake, solitary as a lone bird on a roof.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also watches through the night with no companion but the dark.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the lonely wakeful watch matches well, though the psalm’s affliction is not love.

islam.quote_or_event: “And made your sleep [a means for] rest.”
islam.explanation: Among the signs of God’s care, the Qur’an names sleep, given to all creatures for their rest.
islam.tie_back: The night gives this rest to every living being except the Kural’s heroine, who is left awake.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International); it states the night’s gift of rest to all, which the Kural assumes, but contains nothing of loneliness or love.

judaism.quote_or_event: “She weepeth sore in the night, And her tears are on her cheeks; She hath none to comfort her Among all her lovers.”
judaism.explanation: Lamentations pictures Jerusalem as a woman weeping alone through the night with no one to comfort her.
judaism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s heroine at night: weeping, wakeful, and without any companion.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); a close image of a woman alone and comfortless at night, though the poem mourns a ruined city.

buddhism.quote_or_event: On the night of his renunciation, Prince Siddhartha wakes in the palace to find everyone around him asleep, and leaves while Yasodhara and their newborn son sleep on, so that she wakes to find herself without him.
buddhism.explanation: The Buddhist narrative of the Great Departure is set in a sleeping palace with one figure awake.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s scene is the same night seen from Yasodhara’s side: all others sleep, and the one left behind keeps watch alone.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known narrative, not checked against a translation this session; the sleeping household and the separation match, but the canonical account follows Siddhartha, not Yasodhara’s wakefulness.

jainism.quote_or_event: In the dialogue of Kesi and Gautama, a frightful fire is said to be blazing up and burning embodied beings, and Gautama explains that the fire is the passions, quenched only by knowledge, virtue and penance.
jainism.explanation: Jain teaching describes the passions as a fire that keeps burning those who have not mastered them.
jainism.tie_back: While the night quiets every other being, the heroine alone is kept awake by the burning of her longing.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of verses read on archive.sacred-texts.com this session; the burning passion connects only loosely, and there is no image of night or of solitude.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: A short poem traditionally attributed to Sappho says that the moon has set and the Pleiades, it is midnight, the hour goes by, and the speaker lies alone.
greek_mythology.explanation: The lines catch the precise moment of midnight solitude in a few words.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, the speaker is awake at midnight with no companion but the night.
greek_mythology.source: Sappho (attributed), fragment 168B Voigt, ‘The moon has set’ (paraphrase)
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous fragment whose attribution to Sappho is disputed, not checked against a translation this session; a near match in the midnight solitude of a lover.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Epictetus distinguishes being alone from being forlorn: a forlorn person is one who has lost those he depended on and feels himself abandoned even in a crowd.
philosophy.explanation: Epictetus analyses loneliness as the feeling of being bereft of a needed companion.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s loneliness is of this kind, so complete that she imagines the night itself as her only companion.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the discourse’s main distinction, not checked against Long’s translation this session; it analyses forlornness but counsels self-sufficiency, unlike the Kural.

kurals.tamil:
கொடியார் கொடுமையின் தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள்
நெடிய கழியும் இரா.
kurals.transliteration:
Kotiyaar kodumaiyin thaamkotiya innaal
netiya kazhiyum iraa.
kurals.meaning: These nights that drag on so long are crueller even than the cruelty of the cruel one who left me.
kurals.elementary: When you are waiting for something you really want, like a birthday, the days feel super long. The wife waiting for her husband says the long nights are even meaner to her than her husband was for going away.
kurals.university: The couplet plays on koṭu (கொடு, cruel): koṭiyār (கொடியார், ‘the cruel one’, the departed husband), koṭumai (கொடுமை, cruelty) and koṭiya (கொடிய, cruel) are stacked so that the nights, iṉṉāḷ neṭiya kaḻiyum irā (‘the nights which in these days pass so long’), outdo the husband in cruelty. The comparison lets the heroine blame the nights rather than the husband, softening the reproach of 1165. There is a sandhi variant in the first line: ytamizh.com prints தாம்கொடிய இந்நாள், while thirukkural.net prints தாம்கொடிய விந்நாள், with the glide v of koṭiya + iṉṉāḷ written out; the reading is the same. Pope: ‘More cruel than the cruelty of him, the cruel one, / In these sad times are lengthening hours of night I watch alone.’

hinduism.quote_or_event: In the Meghaduta, the separated yaksha wishes that the night with its long watches could somehow be shortened to a moment, and that his days apart might pass more quickly.
hinduism.explanation: Kalidasa’s lover feels the night of separation stretch out unbearably.
hinduism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine says the same: the long nights of separation are her worst tormentors.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known stanza, not checked against a translation this session; the wish for shorter nights in separation matches closely, though the speaker is the husband.

christianity.quote_or_event: “So am I made to possess months of vanity, and wearisome nights are appointed to me. When I lie down, I say, When shall I arise, and the night be gone? and I am full of tossings to and fro unto the dawning of the day.”
christianity.explanation: Job describes nights that will not end, spent tossing and waiting for dawn.
christianity.tie_back: Job’s wearisome nights are the Kural’s nights that ‘pass so long’, felt as a torment in themselves.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; a close match for nights that seem endless, though Job suffers affliction, not separation.

islam.quote_or_event: “…to the point that the earth closed in on them in spite of its vastness and their souls confined them…”
islam.explanation: The three companions who were shunned after staying behind felt the wide earth itself shrink around them in their anguish.
islam.tie_back: As anguish made the vast earth feel narrow to them, longing makes the heroine’s nights feel endlessly long.
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via the quran.com API (Sahih International), quoted in part; it shares the idea of grief distorting one’s sense of the world, but concerns repentance, not love or time.

judaism.quote_or_event: “In the morning thou shalt say, Would God it were even! and at even thou shalt say, Would God it were morning!”
judaism.explanation: Among the curses of Deuteronomy is a dread so constant that every hour seems too long and the next one is wished for.
judaism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine lives this restlessness at night, when every hour drags and she longs for it to pass.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV (a JPS rendering was not checked this session); it captures time dragging in distress, but the cause is fear under a curse, not love.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Long is the night to the sleepless; long is the league to the weary. Long is worldly existence to fools who know not the Sublime Truth.”
buddhism.explanation: The Dhammapada begins its chapter on the fool by noting how the night stretches out for one who cannot sleep.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine knows exactly this: for the sleepless, the night is long and cruel.
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; the long night of the sleepless is a near match for the couplet’s image, though the verse uses it as a metaphor for samsara.

jainism.quote_or_event: “The day that goes by will never return; the days elapse without profit to him who acts contrary to the Law.”
jainism.explanation: Bhrigu’s sons warn that time spent without the Law is lost; Jacobi notes that the original literally says ‘the nights’, the old way of counting time.
jainism.tie_back: The heroine counts her separation in nights that pass painfully; the Jain verse also counts life in nights, but urges using them for the Law rather than in longing.
jainism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on sacred-texts.com, with Jacobi’s footnote on ‘nights’; the link is the passing of nights, but the Jain verse is about wasted time, not their painful length.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: In the Odyssey, Penelope tells the disguised Odysseus that by day she can find relief in weeping and in her household tasks, but when night comes and all others are asleep, she lies awake with sharp cares crowding her heart.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope finds the nights of her husband’s long absence harder than the days.
greek_mythology.tie_back: Like the Kural’s heroine, Penelope finds the long nights the cruellest part of separation.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known speech, not checked against a translation this session; a near match in a separated wife’s sleepless, painful nights.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Augustine argues that time is measured in the mind itself, so that a ‘long future’ is really a long expectation of the future, stretched out in the soul that waits.
philosophy.explanation: For Augustine, how long time seems depends on the stretching of the waiting mind.
philosophy.tie_back: The heroine’s nights are long because her mind is stretched out in waiting for her husband’s return.
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of Augustine’s analysis of time, not checked against a translation this session; it explains why waiting lengthens time but carries none of the Kural’s emotion.

kurals.tamil:
உள்ளம்போன்று உள்வழிச் செல்கிற்பின் வெள்ளநீர்
நீந்தல மன்னோஎன் கண்.
kurals.transliteration:
Ullampoandru ulvazhich chelkirpin vellaneer
neendhala mannoaen kan.
kurals.meaning: If my eyes could travel like my heart to where he is, they would not have to swim in this flood of tears.
kurals.elementary: Your thoughts can fly anywhere: you can imagine being with your grandma far away in a second. But your eyes cannot go there to see her. The wife says her heart is already with her husband, but her eyes are stuck at home, so they just cry and cry.
kurals.university: The closing couplet contrasts uḷḷam (உள்ளம், heart or mind), which goes freely to uḷvaḻi (உள்வழி, ‘the place where he is’), with kaṇ (கண், the eyes), which cannot follow and so must ‘swim’ (nīntu, நீந்து) in veḷḷa nīr (வெள்ளநீர், a flood of water), that is, tears. Celkiṟpiṉ (செல்கிற்பின்) is ‘if they were able to go’, and maṉṉō (மன்னோ) adds regretful emphasis. Puliyur Kesikan extends the wish to her whole body going where her heart is, while the other glossators keep to the eyes. The flood of this couplet answers the floods of 1164 and 1167: the sea of love has become the water of her own tears, and the next chapter (118, kaṇ vitumpu aḻital) turns entirely to the eyes. Pope: ‘When eye of mine would as my soul go forth to him, / It knows not how through floods of its own tears to swim.’ The text is identical on both base sources.

hinduism.quote_or_event: When Uddhava brings Krishna’s message from Mathura, the gopis of Vraja tell him that their minds are always with Krishna, even though they themselves must remain behind, weeping, in the village.
hinduism.explanation: The gopis’ hearts have gone where Krishna is, but their bodies and eyes are left in Vraja.
hinduism.tie_back: This is the Kural’s contrast exactly: the heart travels to the beloved, while the eyes stay behind in tears.
hinduism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a well-known episode, not checked against a translation this session; the heart-present, body-absent contrast matches, though the gopis’ love is devotional.

christianity.quote_or_event: “I am weary with my groaning; all the night make I my bed to swim; I water my couch with my tears.”
christianity.explanation: The psalmist, in great distress, weeps so much that he says his bed swims in tears.
christianity.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine uses the same hyperbole: her eyes swim in a flood of tears.
christianity._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim via bolls.life KJV; the image of swimming in tears is a striking verbal match, though the psalm’s distress is not about an absent beloved.

islam.quote_or_event: “Ever since they tore me from my osier bed, My plaintive notes have moved men and women to tears. I burst my breast, striving to give vent to sighs, And to express the pangs of my yearning for my home.”
islam.explanation: Rumi’s reed-flute, cut from its reed bed, cries out with longing to return to where it belongs.
islam.tie_back: The reed’s heart is with its home and its body cannot go there, which is the heroine’s situation, and its lament moves others to tears as hers floods her eyes.
islam.source: Rumi, Masnavi, Book 1, Prologue (tr. E.H. Whinfield)
islam._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on archive.sacred-texts.com (Whinfield); the longing to return to an absent home matches, though Rumi’s yearning is mystical and the tears are others’.

judaism.quote_or_event: “For these things I weep; Mine eye, mine eye runneth down with water; Because the comforter is far from me, Even he that should refresh my soul.”
judaism.explanation: The voice of Lamentations weeps endlessly because the one who should bring comfort is far away.
judaism.tie_back: The heroine’s eyes are flooded for the same reason: the one who would comfort her is far off and cannot be reached.
judaism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on Sefaria (JPS 1917); eyes running with water because the comforter is far away is a close match, though the context is national mourning.

buddhism.quote_or_event: “Which is greater, the tears you have shed while transmigrating & wandering this long, long time — crying & weeping from being joined with what is displeasing, being separated from what is pleasing — or the water in the four great oceans?”
buddhism.explanation: The Buddha asks his monks to compare all the tears they have shed over separation with the oceans, and they answer that the tears are greater.
buddhism.tie_back: The Kural’s ‘flood of tears’ shed in separation becomes, in the Buddha’s reckoning, a flood greater than the seas.
buddhism.source: Samyutta Nikaya 15.3, Assu Sutta (tr. Thanissaro Bhikkhu)
buddhism._accuracy_note: Verified verbatim on accesstoinsight.org; tears of separation measured as a flood match the image strongly, though the sutta’s point is disenchantment with samsara.

jainism.quote_or_event: When her betrothed Arishtanemi leaves on their wedding day to become a monk, Princess Rajimati does not stay behind in grief but herself renounces the world and follows him to Mount Raivataka, where he practises austerities.
jainism.explanation: In the Jain story, Rajimati turns her longing into action and goes where her heart has already gone.
jainism.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine wishes she could go where her heart is; Rajimati actually does, though by way of renunciation.
jainism._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the lecture’s narrative, not re-read this session; the woman who follows her departed beloved matches, but her journey is religious and the story does not dwell on tears.

greek_mythology.quote_or_event: Ovid’s Penelope opens her letter to the long-absent Odysseus by begging him not to write back but to come himself.
greek_mythology.explanation: Penelope wants not messages but presence; words and thoughts cannot cross the distance for her.
greek_mythology.tie_back: The Kural’s heroine also knows that thoughts can travel but she cannot, and longs for real presence instead.
greek_mythology._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of a famous opening line, not checked against a translation this session; the longing for real presence over distance matches, but there is no image of the mind travelling or of tears.

philosophy.quote_or_event: Seneca tells Lucilius that he never receives a letter from him without at once feeling in his company, because the mind can be with an absent friend even when the body cannot.
philosophy.explanation: Seneca treats the mind as able to cross distance and make an absent friend present.
philosophy.tie_back: The Kural agrees that the heart travels freely, but laments that the eyes cannot follow, which is why they fill with tears.
philosophy.source: Seneca, Moral Letters to Lucilius, Letter 40 (paraphrase)
philosophy._accuracy_note: Paraphrase of the letter’s opening, not checked against Gummere’s translation this session; it shares the idea of the mind reaching an absent person, but finds it consoling where the Kural finds it painful.
